text: Erectile dysfunction: Erectile dysfunction (ED), also referred to as impotence, is a form of sexual dysfunction in males characterized by the persistent or recurring inability to achieve or maintain a penile erection with sufficient rigidity and duration for satisfactory sexual activity. It is the most common sexual problem in males and can cause psychological distress due to its impact on self-image and sexual relationships.
Genital itching: A presenting complaint characterised by genital itching.
Genital lump: A presenting complaint characterised by genital lump.
Genital rash: A presenting complaint characterised by genital rash.
Genital ulcer: A genital ulcer is an open sore located on the genital area, which includes the vulva, penis, perianal region, or anus. Genital ulcers are most commonly caused by infectious agents.
Testicular pain: Testicular pain is pain perceived in one or both testicles. It may originate from the testis or other structures within the scrotum, and may be acute or chronic.
Testicular swelling: A presenting complaint characterised by testicular swelling.

Urethral discharge: The urethra is the tube that transports urine from the bladder to the urethral meatus of the penis or vulva in placental mammals. In males, it also transports semen through the penis during ejaculation.

Corporo-venous occlusive erectile dysfunction differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Other Male Erectile Dysfunction: Corporo-venous occlusive erectile dysfunction is a specific vascular diagnosis (venous leak preventing erection maintenance), typically confirmed by penile duplex ultrasound; other male erectile dysfunction covers causes without this specific vascular confirmation. Compared to Male Erectile Dysfunction Unspecified: Corporo-venous occlusive erectile dysfunction has objective vascular testing confirming a venous leak; unspecified erectile dysfunction has no such confirmed cause.

Drug-induced erectile dysfunction differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Other Male Erectile Dysfunction: Drug-induced erectile dysfunction has a clear temporal link to starting or changing a medication (e.g., antihypertensives, SSRIs); other male erectile dysfunction has an identified non-drug cause (e.g., vascular, neurogenic, hormonal) that isn't medication. Compared to Male Erectile Dysfunction Unspecified: Drug-induced erectile dysfunction has a documented causative medication; unspecified erectile dysfunction is used when no cause, drug-related or otherwise, has been established.

Erectile dysfunction following radical prostatectomy differential diagnosis notes. Compared to Erectile Dysfunction Following Simple Prostatectomy: Erectile dysfunction following radical prostatectomy follows removal of the prostate and surrounding tissue for cancer (higher nerve-injury risk); following simple prostatectomy follows removal of prostate tissue for benign disease (e.g., BPH), with lower nerve-injury risk. Compared to Erectile Dysfunction Following Radical Cystectomy: Erectile dysfunction following radical prostatectomy follows prostate removal; following radical cystectomy follows bladder removal, which also risks the neurovascular bundles but via a different surgical field and indication (bladder cancer, not prostate cancer). Compared to Erectile Dysfunction Following Urethral Surgery: Erectile dysfunction following radical prostatectomy is linked to pelvic nerve-sparing surgery for prostate cancer; following urethral surgery is linked to procedures on the urethra itself (e.g., stricture repair), a different anatomical mechanism of injury.
